title: 01 · Stack and vocabulary
subtitle: Trace a request from UI to silicon; separate interaction, control, model and compute.
outcomes: Explain L0–L9 without treating it as ten separate processes
Distinguish UI, agent, harness, model server and compute kernel
Locate a failure at the boundary that can actually produce it

topics.name: The ten-layer mental map
topics.problem: A single “AI app” hides multiple owners and failure modes.
topics.explain: L9 presents the task, L8 controls work, L7 connects tools and evidence, L6 exposes the model API, L5 serializes tokens, L4 executes inference, L3 loads model assets, L2 runs compute kernels, L1 provides OS and device services, and L0 supplies hardware. Boundaries are conceptual, not necessarily separate machines.
topics.example: A coding assistant may display a TUI on your laptop but send inference to a remote model server while executing shell commands locally.
topics.tradeoff: Swapping the TUI rarely alters inference quality; swapping tokenizer, context policy or model may.
topics.failure: A user-visible hang could occur in tools, network, queue, first-token latency or UI: trace all owners.

topics.name: Control plane vs compute plane
topics.problem: Model output is not system authority.
topics.explain: The control plane owns tool permissions, approvals, retries, memory, budgets and state; the compute plane predicts tokens. A generated “delete” command does not confer permission to run it.
topics.example: The model proposes an action; the harness checks allowlists and asks a human before execution.
topics.tradeoff: Moving validation into a prompt is simpler but weaker than deterministic authorization outside the model.
topics.failure: A tool ran without approval: investigate the harness/executor, not “model alignment” alone.

topics.name: Three meanings of kernel
topics.problem: The same term means radically different things at different layers.
topics.explain: An OS kernel manages processes, memory and devices. A GPU compute kernel is an operation executed on an accelerator. A Jupyter kernel is a language execution process. They have different security and performance responsibilities.
topics.example: An out-of-memory CUDA kernel and a crashed notebook kernel have different root causes despite sharing a word.
topics.tradeoff: Changing an attention kernel may accelerate inference; updating the OS kernel can alter driver compatibility.
topics.failure: A “kernel error” report without a layer is not diagnostically meaningful.

topics.name: Interfaces do not equal backends
topics.problem: CLI, TUI, IDE and browser are interaction surfaces.
topics.explain: A CLI exposes commands, a TUI provides terminal interaction, an IDE integrates editing, and an HTTP API exposes services. The same harness can serve several frontends, and different frontends can hide different harnesses.
topics.example: A terminal coding agent may invoke the same model provider as a web agent but use different tools and execution permissions.
topics.tradeoff: Replacing the frontend changes ergonomics; replacing the harness changes safety, retries and task completion behavior.
topics.failure: A frontend reports “done” but nothing was written: inspect the harness and filesystem proof.

topics.name: The compatibility triangle
topics.problem: Model weights are not self-describing execution contracts.
topics.explain: Architecture, weights, tokenizer and chat template must match. A serving runtime also needs supported numerical formats, kernels and hardware. “Model loaded” does not prove prompt formatting is correct.
topics.example: A quantized variant can preserve tokenizer and template; a different model family may not.
topics.tradeoff: A mismatched chat template may silently degrade responses rather than trigger an obvious crash.
topics.failure: Sudden tool-call failures after a model swap suggest template and schema compatibility checks.

topics.name: End-to-end proof
topics.problem: A green API status is not evidence that an entire workflow succeeded.
topics.explain: Trace user intent, assembled request, model response, proposed actions, applied policy, tool side effects and validated deliverable. Assign each event an owner and correlation ID.
topics.example: For a file-edit agent, prove the correct file hash, tests, approval, and no unauthorized writes.
topics.tradeoff: More trace detail improves diagnosis but increases retention and privacy obligations.
topics.failure: “Completed” with no artifact or action log is an unproven claim.

title: 02 · Tokens and model mechanics
subtitle: Understand what the model predicts, how prompts become tokens and why outputs vary.
outcomes: Explain tokenization, embeddings, attention, logits and sampling
Distinguish training/fine-tuning from inference
Explain why generated text is not a verified fact

topics.name: Tokenizer and token IDs
topics.problem: Models operate on discrete IDs, not directly on human words.
topics.explain: A tokenizer splits an input into pieces using a vocabulary and a specific algorithm. Spaces, punctuation and multilingual text can change token counts. Token IDs must match the embeddings expected by the model.
topics.example: “Unbelievable” can map to one or several tokens depending on tokenizer and vocabulary.
topics.tradeoff: Swapping tokenizers independently can invalidate embedding semantics and model behavior.
topics.failure: Token counts differ sharply between model families, causing context-budget surprises.

topics.name: Embeddings and parameters
topics.problem: Token IDs become vectors; learned parameters transform them.
topics.explain: Embeddings map IDs to dense numerical representations. The model contains weights learned during training; those weights implement mathematical transformations, not a database of guaranteed statements.
topics.example: The same token can influence later tokens differently depending on surrounding context.
topics.tradeoff: More parameters can improve capacity but increase storage, latency and compute demands; size alone is not quality.
topics.failure: Treating model output as deterministic lookup leads to unsupported confidence.

topics.name: Attention and context
topics.problem: Transformers combine information across sequence positions.
topics.explain: Attention builds context-sensitive representations; it is not literal human attention or a perfect memory. Causal decoding conditions each new token on preceding tokens and the allowed context window.
topics.example: A pronoun may refer to an earlier name, but long or noisy contexts can still confuse the model.
topics.tradeoff: Longer context increases potential evidence but can add KV-cache pressure and distractors.
topics.failure: Failure to use a fact present in context can reflect retrieval, position, formatting or model limits.

topics.name: Logits, sampling and temperature
topics.problem: Generation selects one next token repeatedly.
topics.explain: The model produces scores (logits) over a vocabulary. Decoding transforms these into candidate probabilities, then chooses tokens via greedy search or sampling settings such as temperature and top-p.
topics.example: A low temperature often narrows variability; it does not enforce factuality or tool correctness.
topics.tradeoff: High diversity may aid ideation but can harm reproducibility for strict extraction tasks.
topics.failure: A schema breaks at temperature 0: investigate templates, decoding, validation and model limits.

topics.name: Training vs inference vs fine-tuning
topics.problem: Weights are learned in training and normally held fixed during serving.
topics.explain: Pretraining updates model weights from large datasets. Fine-tuning continues targeted weight updates; inference uses existing weights to produce outputs. Retrieval instead supplies new context without modifying parameters.
topics.example: A local policy document changes every day: retrieval is usually safer than daily fine-tuning.
topics.tradeoff: Fine-tuning can shape behavior but costs data preparation, compute and regression testing.
topics.failure: A model ignoring new policy text is not automatically a reason to retrain it.

topics.name: Hallucination and uncertainty
topics.problem: Fluent text can be unsupported by actual evidence.
topics.explain: Probability of text is not a calibrated probability of truth. Models can generate plausible wrong citations, commands or explanations. Ground answers with evidence and verify actions with external checks.
topics.example: A deployment assistant reports a command succeeded: compare with the actual exit code and service status.
topics.tradeoff: Stronger models help but cannot replace citations, constraints and outcome validation.
topics.failure: High confidence without source evidence must trigger verification rather than trust.

title: 03 · Inference and hardware
subtitle: Follow prefill, decode, KV cache, kernels, quantization and memory constraints.
outcomes: Separate prefill latency from decode throughput
Estimate a KV cache from explicit assumptions
Explain throughput/latency trade-offs and quantization limits

topics.name: Prefill vs decode
topics.problem: Input processing and output generation have different cost profiles.
topics.explain: During prefill the runtime processes prompt tokens and builds attention state; time to first token includes queueing and prefill. During autoregressive decode the system repeatedly emits new tokens, commonly constrained by weight/memory movement.
topics.example: A long retrieved context can slow first response even when output is short.
topics.tradeoff: Optimizing only tokens per second can hide poor time-to-first-token.
topics.failure: A new retriever creates slow requests: inspect input length and prefill, not just network.

topics.name: KV cache
topics.problem: Reuse previous attention keys/values instead of recomputing all past positions.
topics.explain: For a common transformer approximation, KV bytes ≈ 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × bytes/element × sequences. Actual layouts, attention variants and runtime paging vary.
topics.example: For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, dimension 128, 4096 tokens, FP16, one sequence: approximately 0.5 GiB.
topics.tradeoff: Longer contexts and concurrency both grow cache requirements; GQA reduces KV head count.
topics.failure: A model fits at idle but fails with concurrent long requests because KV allocation grows.

topics.name: GPU compute kernels
topics.problem: Tensor operations execute as optimized kernels on accelerators.
topics.explain: Matrix multiplication, normalization and attention use hardware-specific kernels; drivers, runtimes and memory allocators mediate execution. An OS kernel is not the same thing.
topics.example: FlashAttention-style kernels reduce attention memory traffic relative to naive materialization.
topics.tradeoff: Fastest kernel depends on shapes, numerical format, driver support and target hardware.
topics.failure: Unsupported instruction sets or driver mismatches can cause fallback or failures.

topics.name: Quantization
topics.problem: Reduce weight representation precision to save memory and often improve throughput.
topics.explain: Quantization maps values into fewer bits using a format and scale strategy. Actual accuracy impact varies by model, quantization method and workload; KV cache may have its own precision setting.
topics.example: A 4-bit model can fit hardware that cannot serve the uncompressed original.
topics.tradeoff: Lower precision is not always faster on every CPU/GPU and can degrade difficult reasoning.
topics.failure: A quantized model “works” but regresses on domain test cases: compare side-by-side evaluations.

topics.name: Batching and scheduling
topics.problem: Servers improve utilization by combining work across requests.
topics.explain: Static batching joins tasks at one point; continuous batching admits and retires requests during decoding. Prefix caching can reuse shared prompt prefixes when safe and supported.
topics.example: A busy shared endpoint may improve total tokens/sec while individual p95 latency degrades.
topics.tradeoff: Choose scheduling policy against expected arrival rate and tail-latency SLO.
topics.failure: Intermittent queue time spikes despite fast kernels indicate serving pressure.

topics.name: Local versus remote inference
topics.problem: Deployment location shifts responsibility and trust.
topics.explain: Local inference gives more deployment control and can reduce data egress, but requires capacity, security and driver maintenance. Remote inference offers managed capacity and model availability but introduces network, cost and policy dependencies.
topics.example: Sensitive drafts stay on a hardened workstation; high-volume use might need a dedicated server.
topics.tradeoff: Model quality, latency, licensing, costs and data boundary must all be evaluated together.
topics.failure: Assuming “local” automatically means secure omits permissions, logs, model provenance and device controls.

title: 04 · Local deployment and serving
subtitle: Understand model artifacts, runtimes, HTTP serving, driver boundaries and reproducibility.
outcomes: Explain the components of a self-hosted model server
Perform a non-destructive deployment plan and runtime probe
List what must be checked before model/runtime upgrades

topics.name: Model file vs runtime
topics.problem: Weights alone cannot accept and serve requests.
topics.explain: A model artifact contains parameters and metadata; a runtime loads compatible tensors, runs kernels, manages caches and exposes generation functions. A serving layer may add HTTP, queues, multi-tenant admission and telemetry.
topics.example: llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM and SGLang solve overlapping problems but differ in interface, model coverage and scheduling.
topics.tradeoff: Replacing runtime changes formats, resource use, templates, optimizations and failure modes.
topics.failure: A downloaded model file with no compatible backend is not a running service.

topics.name: Serving choices
topics.problem: Select tools for tasks, not popularity.
topics.explain: Desktop apps favor interactive simplicity; single-user runtimes emphasize accessible local inference; throughput servers emphasize scheduling, concurrency and instrumentation. SDK compatibility is another independent dimension.
topics.example: One learner can start with Ollama then benchmark a second backend with the same prompt corpus.
topics.tradeoff: Compare against fixed workload, GPU memory budget, drivers and actual quality—not screenshots.
topics.failure: A server offering a compatible endpoint may still differ in schema and tool-call behavior.

topics.name: Network and process boundary
topics.problem: localhost and remote endpoints have different exposure risks.
topics.explain: A loopback-bound inference server is reachable only from its host under normal networking; binding a service publicly increases attack surface. TLS, identity, quotas and gateway authorization matter for remote access.
topics.example: A workstation accesses a remote model over HTTPS through an authenticated gateway.
topics.tradeoff: Public binding is convenient in a lab but unsafe without access controls and threat modelling.
topics.failure: “It responds with curl” does not prove who else can access the endpoint.

topics.name: Version pinning and compatibility
topics.problem: Reproducibility requires tracking more than the model name.
topics.explain: Record exact model revision/checksum, quantization, tokenizer/template, runtime version, driver, kernels and launch config. Keep a known-good rollback point.
topics.example: A newly updated serving binary changes output structure: compare to a golden request and restore if incompatible.
topics.tradeoff: Automatic updates lower upkeep but may introduce unexpected behavior changes.
topics.failure: A regression with unchanged model weights may still come from runtime or template drift.

topics.name: Hardware topology
topics.problem: Compute and display share limited resources on workstations.
topics.explain: On laptops and hybrid-GPU desktops, inference placement must consider device selection, display use, memory copies, power budgets and thermal limits. CPU execution is possible but throughput differs.
topics.example: An iGPU handles display while a separate accelerator runs inference, if driver/runtime support permits.
topics.tradeoff: Hardware capability does not imply backend kernel support for that precise software revision.
topics.failure: A generic GPU query can select a device different from the one expected.

topics.name: Serving health
topics.problem: A healthy process can still deliver broken answers.
topics.explain: Verify startup, request admission, timeouts, outputs, memory growth, latency, template compatibility and a small known-answer regression set. Monitor both process health and task quality.
topics.example: Send one harmless prompt; verify JSON validity, decoded text and response timing.
topics.tradeoff: More monitoring helps isolation but requires structured retention and privacy policies.
topics.failure: A green /health with malformed output is an application-level failure.

lab.title: Deploy-and-probe plan
lab.goal: Produce a safe, reproducible local-serving runbook; optionally execute on your own sandbox.

steps.title: Design a smoke test

title: 05 · Prompt contracts and context
subtitle: Learn messages, chat templates, context assembly, structured outputs and budget failure.
outcomes: Trace how system/developer/user/tool data enter a model request
Design a schema with deterministic validation and retry limits
Explain why context expansion is not free or always helpful

topics.name: Instruction hierarchy and data provenance
topics.problem: Not every token should carry authority.
topics.explain: System/developer guidance, user requests and retrieved/tool content have different trust roles. The harness owns assembly and must preserve source provenance; lower-trust text cannot grant permissions.
topics.example: A web page saying “ignore earlier instructions” is evidence to summarize, not a new system message.
topics.tradeoff: Concatenating everything as raw text is simple but can erase role/source separation.
topics.failure: An injected page triggers a command: check whether untrusted text was promoted into control instructions.

topics.name: Chat templates
topics.problem: Role structure becomes exact model-facing token sequences.
topics.explain: The tokenizer and chat template map role/message boundaries and control markers to input tokens. Tool-call and reasoning formatting are model/runtime-specific; templates must match serving expectations.
topics.example: A system prompt concatenated as plain user text may behave differently from correctly marked messages.
topics.tradeoff: Changing template can alter safety, tool use and output formatting even with fixed weights.
topics.failure: A previously valid tool call fails after a model switch: audit serialization first.

topics.name: Context window vs useful evidence
topics.problem: Maximum tokens and effective task attention are different.
topics.explain: A context window is the upper bound of model-visible tokens. The useful subset depends on relevance, ordering, attention behavior and output allocation. Pasting entire repositories often reduces signal.
topics.example: A coding task benefits more from two relevant files than from thousands of unrelated lines.
topics.tradeoff: Summarization saves tokens but may discard constraints; retrieval needs relevance checks.
topics.failure: Correct evidence exists in context but the model misses it: test ordering and chunk selection.

topics.name: Structured outputs
topics.problem: A request for JSON is not a validated typed object.
topics.explain: Define an output schema, validate generated data outside the model, handle missing/extra fields and bound retries. Tool argument schemas and final output schemas serve different consumers.
topics.example: Return {"status":"ok","count":3} only when field types pass a deterministic validator.
topics.tradeoff: Strict validation adds rejection/retry costs but reduces silent downstream corruption.
topics.failure: Invalid values reaching a database indicate missing enforcement after generation.

topics.name: Truncation and compression
topics.problem: Context budgets must include instructions, history, tools and output.
topics.explain: Trimming naive “oldest first” can remove decisions or safety constraints; selective summarization and state checkpoints preserve essential facts. History is not persistent memory unless saved and restored.
topics.example: Keep an architecture decision record while compacting old chat turns.
topics.tradeoff: Compression improves fit but creates information-loss risk; measure task regressions.
topics.failure: Agent repeats already-resolved work after compaction: inspect what state was retained.

topics.name: Prompt caching and cost
topics.problem: Stable prefixes may be reused to reduce repeated computation where supported.
topics.explain: Prefix caching is a serving/runtime capability with exact-match and policy constraints. Small changes to stable instructions or tool catalogs can invalidate cache reuse.
topics.example: Order tools consistently rather than shuffling their definitions every request.
topics.tradeoff: Caching improves latency/cost but requires isolation to avoid cross-tenant leakage.
topics.failure: First-token latency increases after a harmless prompt refactor: check cache hit changes.

lab.goal: Design a prompt contract that keeps evidence separate from authority.

steps.title: Define an output
steps.detail: Use a short two-field JSON summary with evidence IDs. Define exact required keys and maximum lengths.

steps.title: Mark trust
steps.detail: Write a sample system task, user request and untrusted retrieved paragraph; identify which can authorize action.

steps.detail: Define rejection conditions for missing evidence IDs, unexpected keys and invalid field types.

steps.title: Try an injection

lab.safety: Use synthetic inputs only; do not expose real API keys, internal files, or personal data.

title: 06 · Agents, harnesses and patterns
subtitle: Turn model proposals into bounded, observable workflows rather than autonomous guesses.
outcomes: Define model vs agent vs harness precisely
Choose fixed workflow, routing, ReAct or planner patterns rationally
Specify approval, recovery, termination and budgets

topics.name: Model, agent and harness
topics.problem: Differentiate generation, deciding, and execution.
topics.explain: A model produces candidate tokens. An agent is a goal-directed process that uses model decisions and tools. A harness provides the surrounding loop: context, tool mediation, limits, retries, logging, permissions, state and result verification.
topics.example: Same model in two coding agents can behave differently because their harnesses select files, run tests and seek approval differently.
topics.tradeoff: Changing a model does not automatically fix missing rollback or excessive tool access.
topics.failure: Repeated tool calls without a stop rule indicate loop governance failure.

topics.name: Fixed workflows before open loops
topics.problem: Not every problem needs autonomy.
topics.explain: A deterministic pipeline is easier to test, audit and cost-control. Routing lets one of several predefined paths run. Dynamic agent loops are useful when next steps cannot be enumerated safely.
topics.example: Invoice OCR → validate → human approve is a workflow; exploratory bug diagnosis may need a bounded agent.
topics.tradeoff: Agent flexibility raises variance, prompt-injection exposure and nontermination risk.
topics.failure: A simple extraction app using a free-running agent is probably over-engineered.

topics.name: ReAct and plan-execute
topics.problem: Agents can reason about next actions, then observe outcomes.
topics.explain: In a ReAct-style loop the model alternates tool selection and observation. Planner-executor separates high-level plan from actions and may introduce independent verification. Neither pattern guarantees correctness.
topics.example: The executor calls test runner after editing; verifier compares diff and test exit codes.
topics.tradeoff: Planning can improve multi-step coordination but adds latency and plan-drift concerns.
topics.failure: An agent follows stale plan despite changed state: require replanning gates and fresh observations.

topics.name: State, recovery and resumability
topics.problem: A resilient harness must survive partial progress.
topics.explain: Persist task IDs, completed actions, approvals, observations and idempotency keys. Retry only safe operations; external side effects may not be repeatable. Keep partial failures visible.
topics.example: An API create request times out after sending: query by idempotency key before retrying.
topics.tradeoff: Durable state costs storage and complexity but avoids duplicate side effects.
topics.failure: Duplicate VMs appear after a timeout: likely at-least-once execution without reconciliation.

topics.name: Budgets and termination
topics.problem: Bound both resource consumption and authority.
topics.explain: Cap maximum steps, wall time, token budget, tool retries and risk categories. Define what counts as success, failure or escalation. A verifier should inspect actual outputs, not generated claims.
topics.example: Stop a coding loop after three repair attempts and report failing tests.
topics.tradeoff: Tighter budgets improve predictability but may reject legitimate complex tasks.
topics.failure: A task spins indefinitely despite no new observations: terminate and surface failure.

topics.name: Coding harness anatomy
topics.problem: A code-editing agent is an engineering control system.
topics.explain: Inputs include repo state and task spec; tools read/edit code and run tests; approvals gate sensitive execution; checkpoints enable rollback; output is a diff, tests and review evidence.
topics.example: A TUI may show a patch while harness maintains sandbox state and collected test results.
topics.tradeoff: Broad filesystem access speeds work but increases blast radius; scope to workspace and commands.
topics.failure: A patch exists but branch checks fail: output cannot be called complete.

lab.title: Design a bounded agent as a state machine
lab.goal: Create a tool-using agent design that cannot silently exceed budget or permissions.

steps.title: Define the task
steps.detail: Use “repair a small Markdown link list” in a sandbox directory. State allowed edits and stop conditions.

steps.title: Draw states
steps.detail: Define PLAN, READ, PROPOSE, APPROVE, APPLY, TEST, DONE, FAILED and allowed transitions.
steps.code: PLAN -> READ -> PROPOSE -> APPROVE -> APPLY -> TEST -> DONE

steps.title: Specify limits
steps.detail: Set max iterations, tools, wall time and user approval required before external writes.

steps.title: Simulate failure
steps.detail: What happens when tests fail twice or a file changes concurrently? Specify reconcile/retry/abort.

lab.evidence: A state diagram, policy table, failure transition and unambiguous definition of DONE.
lab.stretch: Compare a fixed two-tool workflow to your agent and justify the autonomy premium.
lab.safety: Use synthetic inputs only; do not expose real API keys, internal files, or personal data.

title: 07 · Tools, MCP, APIs and A2A
subtitle: Connect systems with explicit contracts and identity boundaries.
outcomes: Distinguish tool call, HTTP API, MCP, SDK and A2A
Explain who validates arguments and authorizes operations
Design a narrow, observable tool boundary

topics.name: Tool calling vs direct execution
topics.problem: The model proposes arguments; an executor makes effects real.
topics.explain: A tool description/schema helps the model form a candidate action. The host/harness must validate values, enforce identity, authorize effects and handle error paths before invoking code.
topics.example: A proposed “search_file” call is read-only; a proposed “delete_file” needs explicit scope and approval.
topics.tradeoff: Tool availability is not permission; model-generated arguments are still untrusted.
topics.failure: A tool executes outside allowed path: investigate executor scope and path checks.

topics.name: HTTP APIs, SDKs and CLI
topics.problem: These are access mechanisms, not agent protocols by themselves.
topics.explain: HTTP APIs expose network operations; SDKs package client behavior; CLIs provide executable commands. An agent harness can wrap any of these as tools, but then owns timeout, schema, retries and credentials.
topics.example: The same backup service can be invoked through a Python SDK or a CLI wrapper.
topics.tradeoff: CLI wrappers may be easy to start but require robust quoting and environment isolation.
topics.failure: Shell injection through concatenated arguments is a tool design failure, not a tokenizer issue.

topics.name: MCP host, client and server
topics.problem: MCP standardizes discovery and invocation of external capabilities.
topics.explain: The host is the AI application, clients manage connections, servers expose tools, resources and prompts. MCP does not automatically enforce business authorization or make returned content trustworthy.
topics.example: An editor host connects to a read-only repository MCP server exposing file resources.
topics.tradeoff: Standard transport improves interoperability but creates credential, scope and trust decisions.
topics.failure: A newly discovered MCP tool receiving all permissions by default is unsafe.

topics.name: MCP versioning matters
topics.problem: Protocol behavior changes across published revisions.
topics.explain: As of the 2026-07-28 specification, the core protocol adopts stateless requests with per-request metadata and new routing headers. Implementations pinned to older SDKs can still require different initialization/session patterns; check negotiated compatibility before copying snippets.
topics.example: The “initialize” flow from an older tutorial may not match a newer stateless server.
topics.tradeoff: Protocol upgrades can break clients, caches, auth and transports independently of model behavior.
topics.failure: A connection fails after SDK upgrade: inspect protocol revision and capability support.

topics.name: A2A vs MCP
topics.problem: Inter-agent delegation differs from calling a specific tool.
topics.explain: MCP focuses on application-to-capability interaction. A2A describes collaboration/delegation between agents with task-oriented discovery and messaging. Neither is inherently required for a single-agent system.
topics.example: Use MCP to read a document; use A2A when a specialized external agent must own a delegated subtask.
topics.tradeoff: Adding an A2A hop increases coordination, privacy and reliability complexity.
topics.failure: A simple database lookup routed to a second agent creates unnecessary failure boundaries.

topics.name: Least privilege and tool provenance
topics.problem: Identity, data integrity and observability must survive the hop.
topics.explain: Separate connection identity, user delegation, service privileges and per-operation authorization. Log correlation IDs, sanitized arguments and outcomes. Treat resource content as lower-trust data.
topics.example: A tool returns “Run sudo” inside a log result: the harness may quote it but cannot execute it on that basis.
topics.tradeoff: Stricter scopes reduce blast radius but can limit unattended automation.
topics.failure: Audit logs show successful model tool selection but no authorized tool result: distinguish proposal from execution.

lab.title: Specify a minimal read-only tool contract
lab.goal: Design an interoperable tool without granting it broad filesystem access.

steps.title: Choose one capability
steps.detail: Define get_status(service_name) with allowed names, output fields and errors.

steps.title: Define scope
steps.detail: Bind authorized service names and credentials in the host, not inside model text.

steps.title: Write negative cases
steps.detail: Test unknown service, malformed arguments, denied user and timeout. Specify results.

steps.title: Map MCP parties
steps.detail: Identify host, client, server and who owns authorization in your design.

lab.evidence: A tool schema, allowlist/identity decision, four negative tests and a request/response trace.
lab.stretch: Add a delegated-task option and explain why A2A is or is not justified.
lab.safety: Use synthetic inputs only; do not expose real API keys, internal files, or personal data.

title: 08 · Retrieval and memory
subtitle: Ground answers in retrieved evidence and distinguish vector search from durable state.
outcomes: Describe a RAG pipeline end to end
Differentiate embeddings, vector search, reranking and generated citation
Explain why retrieval quality is a separate evaluation target

topics.name: RAG is evidence injection
topics.problem: Retrieval adds relevant facts without changing the model weights.
topics.explain: A retrieval system selects documents or chunks at query time, then passes relevant passages to generation with provenance. It helps answer time-sensitive or private-domain questions but can still retrieve bad evidence.
topics.example: Use a versioned policy document in context rather than training that text into weights.
topics.tradeoff: RAG adds indexing, permissions, relevance and source-version management.
topics.failure: A confidently wrong answer can originate from irrelevant passages or faulty synthesis.

topics.name: Chunking and metadata
topics.problem: Document segmentation determines what can be found.
topics.explain: Split documents along meaningful boundaries, preserve source IDs, titles, timestamps and access controls. Tiny chunks lose context; giant chunks add noise and prompt cost.
topics.example: Chunk each API section with heading and version in metadata so search retrieves the right revision.
topics.tradeoff: Chunk overlap improves continuity but increases index size and duplicate retrieval.
topics.failure: Answer contains fragments without definitions: chunk granularity may be too small.

topics.name: Embeddings and hybrid retrieval
topics.problem: Similarity is not the same as truth or relevance.
topics.explain: Embeddings represent texts in a vector space, enabling approximate semantic search. Keyword/BM25-style retrieval preserves exact tokens, identifiers and error codes; hybrid search can combine both.
topics.example: A precise error string is often better found by lexical search than vague semantic similarity.
topics.tradeoff: ANN/vector indexes add approximate recall tradeoffs and resource costs.
topics.failure: Relevant file missed despite exact error string: check lexical indexing and filters.

topics.name: Reranking and grounding
topics.problem: Selecting the best evidence is a separate stage from writing.
topics.explain: Rerankers score candidate passages for a query; filters can enforce recency, authorization and source quality. The generator should cite evidence IDs that are verified against the retrieved set.
topics.example: An answer claims “policy changed yesterday” only if the retrieved revision supports it.
topics.tradeoff: Extra reranking may improve precision but adds latency and cost.
topics.failure: A citation links to a document that does not contain the claim: validate source spans.

topics.name: Memory types
topics.problem: Chat history, working state and durable memory are distinct.
topics.explain: Conversation context is temporary model input. Task state stores workflow progress. Long-term memory stores explicit durable facts under retention and consent rules. A vector store alone is not a reliable transaction log.
topics.example: Store completed deployment IDs in a database rather than hoping the LLM remembers them from chat.
topics.tradeoff: Persistence improves continuity but can become stale, private or contaminated.
topics.failure: Agent repeats an operation after restart: persistent state and reconciliation may be missing.

topics.name: RAG evaluation
topics.problem: Separate search quality, answer quality and authorization.
topics.explain: Measure retrieval recall@k on labeled queries, precision/relevance, groundedness of claims and citation support. Add permission-aware negative cases; high search recall alone does not guarantee good answers.
topics.example: A benchmark contains question, gold supporting chunk, expected answer and forbidden sources.
topics.tradeoff: Better retrieval can increase model prefill and cost; tune end-to-end metrics.
topics.failure: A high automatic answer score with wrong citations reveals an evaluation gap.

lab.title: Build a tiny evidence-grounded retrieval exercise
lab.goal: Use three synthetic documents to audit selection, citations and access control.

steps.title: Create corpus
steps.detail: Write 3 short fictitious versioned policies; give each an ID and owner.
steps.code:
doc_id,version,allowed_roles,text
P1,v1,all,Sample policy one
P2,v2,staff,Sample policy two

steps.title: Author questions
steps.detail: Write one exact-ID lookup, one paraphrase and one access-denied query.

steps.title: Specify retrieval
steps.detail: Choose lexical or semantic retrieval per query and state why; document candidate IDs.

steps.title: Verify claims

title: 09 · Evaluation, security and trust
subtitle: Prove outcomes and enforce boundaries when model text, tools and data are adversarial.
outcomes: Design reproducible quality and regression evals
Differentiate prompt injection from authorized instruction
Enforce least privilege, approvals and failure isolation

topics.name: Evaluations vs demos
topics.problem: One success story cannot estimate reliability.
topics.explain: An evaluation is a repeatable measurement over representative cases with specified scoring and documented inputs. Use held-out scenarios, regression sets, negative tests and human review where subjective judgment matters.
topics.example: A coding agent must pass unit tests, diff checks, authorization checks and failure scenarios.
topics.tradeoff: More test cases cost time; unrepresentative cases create false confidence.
topics.failure: A model upgrade “feels better” but breaks a rare permission case: add regression evidence.

topics.name: Metric choice
topics.problem: Accuracy, groundedness, latency and cost are separate axes.
topics.explain: A correct answer can be too slow, an inexpensive answer can violate policy, and a fast answer can cite wrong evidence. Report dimensions separately and tie thresholds to business needs.
topics.example: For extraction measure field correctness; for RAG measure citation support; for agents measure task completion and unsafe side effects.
topics.tradeoff: Aggregating everything into one score hides unacceptable tails.
topics.failure: Average quality high but sensitive cases fail: use slice-based metrics.

topics.name: Prompt injection is a trust boundary attack
topics.problem: Untrusted content tries to become instructions.
topics.explain: Web pages, repo files, tool results and retrieved documents may contain malicious instructions. Defensive architecture limits privileges and data flow regardless of whether the model obeys hostile content.
topics.example: A README tells the agent to send secrets to a URL. The harness treats it as untrusted document text.
topics.tradeoff: A prompt saying “ignore injections” helps but cannot replace scoped tools and output validation.
topics.failure: If lower-trust text causes privilege escalation, investigate tool permissions and workflow policy.

topics.name: Threat model of an agent
topics.problem: External side effects amplify small mistakes.
topics.explain: Map assets, identities, entry points, untrusted surfaces, trust boundaries and allowed operations. Consider exfiltration, tool misuse, resource exhaustion, output corruption and supply-chain content.
topics.example: A web-browsing agent with network and filesystem access needs a clearly defined data egress policy.
topics.tradeoff: Sandboxing isolates environments but does not by itself guarantee no network exfiltration.
topics.failure: The agent performed a forbidden write even though its chat response looked harmless.

topics.name: Human approval and deterministic gates
topics.problem: Approval must happen at the action boundary.
topics.explain: Separate “model asked user” from “executor blocked until authorized.” Require approval for destructive changes, credential access or external effects; log who authorized precisely what.
topics.example: A tool call with an unsafe path is denied even when the model says it is urgent.
topics.tradeoff: More gates reduce risk but can add latency and user fatigue; apply risk tiers.
topics.failure: An approve dialog appears after the write: the approval point is incorrectly placed.

topics.name: Observability and incident proof
topics.problem: Trace what ran, not what the assistant claims ran.
topics.explain: Log correlation IDs, model/version, budgets, non-sensitive input metadata, tool attempts, policy decisions, validation and final outcome. Define retention and redaction; secret values should not enter routine logs.
topics.example: A failed job can be reconstructed without printing credentials or full private documents.
topics.tradeoff: Detailed telemetry increases risk if it retains prompts, secrets and retrieved private data.
topics.failure: Without task-to-tool trace correlation, reliability incidents become guesswork.

lab.title: Red-team a synthetic agent workflow
lab.goal: Create an attack/defense table grounded in the architecture rather than slogans.

steps.title: Declare trust map
steps.detail: Mark user instruction, web content, tool responses and tool executor authority.

steps.title: Write 3 attacks
steps.detail: Create harmless synthetic prompt-injection strings in a fake web page, repo README and tool response.

steps.title: Design controls
steps.detail: For each attack identify prevention, detection, audit evidence and permitted fallback.

steps.title: Define evaluation
steps.detail: Set at least 5 pass/fail cases: correct task, denial, invalid input, timeout and attempted exfiltration.

lab.evidence: An attack matrix with three explicit trust boundaries and at least five measurable regression cases.
lab.stretch: Compare failure modes for a no-tools chatbot versus a privileged coding agent.
lab.safety: Use synthetic inputs only; do not expose real API keys, internal files, or personal data.

title: 10 · Production decisions and capstones
subtitle: Choose architectures using evidence; operate within latency, cost, safety and lifecycle constraints.
outcomes: Compare two plausible system designs against one workload
Define SLOs, cost and failure budgets with measured evidence
Complete a reviewable capstone with reproducible rollback

topics.name: Architecture is a trade-off ledger
topics.problem: No tool or model is “best” independently of requirements.
topics.explain: Describe workload, data boundary, concurrency, output quality, latency targets, hardware and cost before choosing a model, runtime or harness. Keep assumptions and rollback explicit.
topics.example: A low-volume internal assistant may value control and simplicity over maximal serving throughput.
topics.tradeoff: A superior benchmark result does not guarantee better task completion or operating cost.
topics.failure: A design recommendation with no workload assumptions is unsupported.

topics.name: SLOs and tail behavior
topics.problem: Averages can hide the user experience.
topics.explain: Define SLI measurements such as TTFT, end-to-end p95 latency, failure rate, valid tool-call rate and grounded-answer proportion. Assign thresholds and measurement periods; track separate slices.
topics.example: “95% of simple requests finish within 4 seconds” is more actionable than “fast enough.”
topics.tradeoff: Stricter SLOs increase capacity costs and may motivate queue limits or caching.
topics.failure: Mean latency stable while p95 deteriorates: inspect bursts, queues and slow-tool tails.

topics.name: Cost and capacity model
topics.problem: Tokens, compute and engineering time are all resources.
topics.explain: Estimate input/output token cost, model memory, utilization, batch behavior, storage, energy, operator time, licensing and reliability cost. Local vs API break-even changes by volume and quality.
topics.example: Budget 1000 daily requests with measured token mix and benchmark latency at real concurrency.
topics.tradeoff: A cheaper inference endpoint may cost more overall if it requires retries or human rework.
topics.failure: Reported cost excludes failed attempts, context growth or engineer operations.

topics.name: Deployment gates and rollback
topics.problem: Reproducible change requires before/after proof.
topics.explain: Capture current state, pin dependencies and model artifacts, define measurable acceptance, stage rollout, observe negative cases and preserve rollback. A claimed successful deploy without tested output is incomplete.
topics.example: Pin runtime/model/template combination and run golden tool-call tests before wider exposure.
topics.tradeoff: Fast auto-rollouts reduce friction but amplify regression risk without gates.
topics.failure: A live endpoint is healthy but wrong model version is loaded: add immutable version evidence.

topics.name: Capstone requirements
topics.problem: A portfolio proves integrated engineering, not isolated prompts.
topics.explain: Ship a bounded tool assistant, grounded document QA, safe coding workflow or inference benchmark. Include architecture diagram, threat model, evaluation dataset, metrics, failures and rollback.
topics.example: A policy assistant returns supported citations and denies unauthorized document retrieval.
topics.tradeoff: Breadth helps but evidence quality matters more than framework count.
topics.failure: A demo lacking logs, tests and failure cases is a prototype, not production proof.

topics.name: Specialization and continued learning
topics.problem: The goal is defensible judgment, not memorizing packages.
topics.explain: After foundations, specialize in model internals, inference systems, orchestration, retrieval, safety or operations. Keep an architecture decision record and revisit it when model/tool versions change.
topics.example: Compare two serving strategies and explain where one stops being economically or operationally valid.
topics.tradeoff: Newer tools can alter options; focus on stable interfaces, measurement and threat boundaries.
topics.failure: Confidence without measurement or rollback is a signal to revisit assumptions.
